News.title: Teenage girl and man in his 20s die in horror crash after car smashes into tree as cops launch appeal
News.content:
TRAGIC SMASH Teenage girl and man in his 20s die in horror crash after car smashes into tree as cops launch appeal

A TEENAGE girl and a man in his 20s died in a horror crash which saw the car smash into a tree.

The tragic incident happened yesterday at around 6pm on the border of Northumberland and Durham.



Cops say the Volkswagen Polo left the road and collided with a tree.

Both occupants – a man in his 20s and a woman in her late teens – tragically passed away at the scene.



The third occupant of the Volkswagen – a man also in his 20s – was taken to hospital for treatment.

He remains there and is said to be in a stable condition.

Both the man and woman’s next of kin have been informed.

Northumbria Police’s Road Policing Unit (RPU) has launched an investigation to determine the full circumstances surrounding the collision.



They are asking anyone who may have witnessed what took place to come forward and speak with them.

Sergeant Craig Bartle said: “Our thoughts are firmly with the family and loved ones of the man and woman who have sadly died as a result of this road traffic incident.

“We will continue to offer their loved ones all of the support they need as we begin our investigations and seek to provide them with answers.”

Sgt Bartle added: “We are now appealing for any information and in particular, anyone with dashcam footage of the incident, or the moments leading up to it.



“We are particularly keen to speak with anyone who was travelling in the area in either direction and who may have seen what happened.

“If this was you, or you were in the area around the time of this collision, please come forward and speak with us.

“Any information you are able to provide could prove crucial to our enquiries.”

Anyone with information or footage is urged to get in touch with the force.

News.title: Woman ‘sexually assaulted’ inside city centre Irish pub as cops share CCTV image of man they want to speak to
News.content:
BAR ATTACK Woman ‘sexually assaulted’ inside city centre Irish pub as cops share CCTV image of man they want to speak to

COPS have released a CCTV image of a man they want to speak to in connection with a sexual assault inside an Irish bar.

It follows reports that a woman was attacked by a man at Katie O’Brien’s Irish Tavern in the Sheffield city centre.





The alleged sexual assault is said to have happened at around 12.50am inside the busy pub last Wednesday, March 8.

Cops say enquiries into the incident are ongoing.

The force has now issued an image of a man they believe could help with their investigation.

Officers admitted the CCTV picture is not of the highest quality.



But they hope the image could jog the memories of anyone who was in the bar or indeed was nearby at the time.

The man they want to trace is described as white, around 5ft 8ins to 5ft 10ins tall.

He is said to be of slim build, with short grey or brown hair.

Cops added that he was wearing a grey jacket.



A South Yorkshire Police spokesperson said: “We are releasing a CCTV image of a man we would like to speak to in connection with reports of a sexual assault inside a Sheffield bar.

“It is reported that on 8 March at 12.50am, a woman was sexually assaulted by a man at Katie O’Brien’s Irish Tavern.

“Enquiries are ongoing and we are now releasing a CCTV image of a man we would like to speak to as we believe they may be able to help us with our investigation.

“We appreciate the image is not of the highest quality, but we hope it may help to jog people’s memories if they were in the venue or surrounding area at the time.”

Anyone with information is urged to contact police online or by calling 101, quoting investigation number 14/47920/26.

News.title: Workers face having pay docked for calling in sick in Germany – where average employee takes over TWO WEEKS off a year
News.content:
SICKIE CRACKDOWN Workers face having pay docked for calling in sick in Germany – where average employee takes over TWO WEEKS off a year

WORKERS in Germany will want to think twice before ringing in sick as they could have sick pay slashed in a new crackdown to “toughen” the workforce.

It comes as employees in Germany take an average of 14.8 sick days per year – one of the highest in Europe.





Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s sick-leave smackdown hopes to beat the soaring numbers of workers taking days of work.

In his 2025 election campaign, Merz vowed to crack down on spiralling sick leave.

He was practically tearing his hair out at his country’s two-week sick leave rate.



In covert talks revealed by newspaper Bild, the ruling centre-Right Christian Democrats (CDU) party and their coalition partner are thinking of docking wages for workers calling in sick.

Under the new plans, workers who ring in sick five times or less could be rewarded with an extra day off.

The rate of sick leave is three times higher than the British average, which came in at around 4.4 days a year in 2024.

The wage-cutting proposals aim to stop workers taking days off for trivial sicknesses like colds.



Merz has previously lashed out at four-day work weeks and work-life balance as he warned Germans that they must work harder to support the country’s ailing economy.

What are sick leave rules in the UK? FROM April 6, workers in the UK are paid wages from the first day taken off for illness. Pay amounts to £123.25 per week, or 80 per cent of earnings if this is lower. Workers must notify employers and a sick note, issued by a doctor, is required for sick leave longer than seven days. Sick leave pay can be shelled out for up to 28 weeks of absence.

The CDU voted to ban workers from phoning in sick in order to boost productivity levels earlier this year.

Workers can be signed off work on sick leave for up to five days by speaking to their doctor on the phone and asking for a sick note.

However, the CDU have been pushing for employees to visit a doctor’s office in person to get signed off.

Germany’s trade union confederation has slammed the plans, as it puts workers “under suspicion” and encourages seniors to treat staff like “shirkers and slackers”.



It comes as Germany ups the ante in preparing to face off Russia.

New guidance from the government forbids working age German men from leaving the country for three months or more without permission from the German army.

Restricting the movements of men of fighting age comes as the country is preparing for a potential Russian attack on NATO within the next two to three years.

News.title: Sick thug who left girlfriend in wheelchair after hurling her from 40ft tower block laughs as he’s jailed
News.content:
A SICK thug who left his girlfriend with horror injuries after he hurled her from a 40ft tower block laughed as he was jailed today.

Bobbie Goodman, 18, was shoved four storeys to the ground below by Jordan Herring and was temporarily left in a wheelchair.





The teen miraculously landed on a grass verge in Solihull, West Midlands, and not a concrete path a couple of feet away that could have killed her.

Bobbie suffered life-changing injuries including a smashed spine, broken ribs, shattered pelvis and a collapsed lung.

Sickingly, Herring maintained that his then-girlfriend jumped – despite there being an hour’s wait before a 999 call was made.

The thug showed no remorse today as he was jailed for five years and laughed as the sentence was handed down.

Herring, 22, was found guilty of unlawful wounding but was cleared of more serious offences of attempted murder and inflicting grievous bodily harm with intent.

He was also convicted of controlling and coercive behaviour against Bobbie after a campaign of abuse leading up to the push.

The court heard Herring had launched into the attack in a cannabis-fuelled rage after interrogating Bobbie about her Snapchat messages.



He had taken the teen to his mum’s house to evade her concerned family, who had been looking for her.

She was already “battered and bruised” with two black eyes and marks to her neck when she arrived at the tower block, it was said.

Shocking CCTV showed her plunging 40ft as Herring refused to give her CPR or call for help.

He also threatened his mum with a knife to prevent her calling emergency services, which she ultimately did not do for one hour and 20 minutes.

Herring then lied to the police – claiming Bobbie jumped from the window in a suicide attempt.



Recalling the horror, she told officers the thug held her near the window and threatened: “I will throw you out, I will kill you.”

In a victim impact statement, Bobbie, now 21, said: “What Herring did to me has affected me in many ways.

“I am extremely lucky to be alive.

News.title: Why is Trump blocking the Strait of Hormuz? What the Iran blockade actually means and why the UK isn’t involved
News.content:
DONALD Trump has launched a naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz – the narrow waterway a fifth of the world’s oil usually passes through every day.

The move has raised the stakes in the struggle for control over the essential energy chokepoint and risks putting the two-week ceasefire deal under even greater strain.





What is the Strait of Hormuz and why does it matter?

The Strait of Hormuz is the vital shipping lane a fifth of the world’s oil passes through.

President Donald Trump has been hell-bent on reopening it since Iran effectively closed it at the end of February.

The US Navy has cut off the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea east of the strait, preventing Iran from profiting off oil and gas exports.

US Central Command has warned that any Iranian-linked vessel daring to break into the waterway would be subject to “interception or capture”.

The blockade applies to all vessels, regardless of flag, though it will only be enforced “partially” on ships going to and from Iranian ports.

US Central Command confirmed: “The blockade will not impede neutral transit passage through the Strait of Hormuz to or from non-Iranian destinations.”

UK Maritime Trade Operations confirmed that neutral vessels will get a “limited grace period” to leave, but it didn’t specify for how long.



Why has Trump launched the blockade?

The blockade follows 21 hours of failed peace talks in Pakistan, where the US and Iran could not resolve their central disagreement – Tehran’s insistence that it will not completely abandon its nuclear programme.

This was the primary catalyst for Trump launching Operation Epic Fury in February.

Iran accused the US of arriving with “excessive demands” and “unlawful requests.”

Leaving Islamabad on Air Force Two, Vice President JD Vance said: “Do we see a fundamental commitment of will for the Iranians not to develop a nuclear weapon… for the long term? We haven’t seen that yet.”

Trump had already criticised Tehran for charging a $2million (£1.5million) fee on every oil tanker that passed through the strait.



He wrote on Truth Social: “Iran will not be allowed to profit off this Illegal Act of EXTORTION. They want money and, more importantly, they want Nuclear.”

Iran previously called the threat of a blockade “ridiculous and laughable”, with its Revolutionary Guard insisting the strait was within its control.

On Monday, April 13, the tone shifted, with a military spokesperson calling the restrictions “piracy” and warning that no Persian Gulf port would be safe for as long as the siege continues.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu threw his support behind Trump’s approach.

He told his cabinet: “The breakdown came from the American side, which could not tolerate Iran’s blatant violation of the terms for entering negotiations.



“The agreement was that there would be a ceasefire, and that the Iranians would immediately open the strait. They did not do so. The Americans could not accept this.”

After the blockade began, Trump returned to social media to warn: “Iran’s Navy is laying at the bottom of the sea, completely obliterated – 158 ships.

“What we have not hit are their small number of, what they call, ‘fast attack ships,’ because we did not consider them much of a threat.

“Warning: If any of these ships come anywhere close to our BLOCKADE, they will be immediately ELIMINATED, using the same system of kill that we use against the drug dealers on boats at Sea.



“It is quick and brutal. P.S. 98.2% of Drugs coming into the US by Ocean or Sea have STOPPED!”

Why is the UK not involved?

Prime Minister Keir Starmer has made clear that Britain will not be part of the blockade.

He said that the UK will not get “dragged in” to the conflict — a position that has put the special relationship between London and Washington under serious strain.

Speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live, Starmer said: “What we’ve been doing over the last few weeks – and this was part of what I was discussing with the Gulf states last week – is bringing countries together to keep the strait open, not shut.”

He added: “We’re not supporting the blockade and all of the marshalling diplomatically, politically and capability.



“We do have mine-sweeping capability, I won’t go into operational matters, but we do have that capability – that’s all focused, from our point of view, on getting the strait fully open.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Following the failed peace talks, sources told the Wall Street Journal that Trump is weighing up a return to military strikes.

Trump told Fox News: “I would hate to do it, but it’s their water, their desalinization [sic] plants, their electric-generating plants, which are very easy to hit.”

News.title: Chilling clues that unlocked case of OAP stabbed in the neck & set alight…11 yrs after cops ruled death a freak accident
News.content:
TRAGIC MISTAKES Chilling clues that unlocked case of OAP stabbed in the neck & set alight…11 yrs after cops ruled death a freak accident

WHEN the body of widow Una Crown was found in the hallway of her bungalow, by her distraught niece Judith, police were called to the scene.

But, spotting a charred tea towel in the kitchen and burns to her body, officers concluded that the 86-year-old, from Wisbech, Cambridgeshire, had accidentally set herself alight on her oven and had probably suffered a heart attack.





Incredibly, wounds on her neck were put down to damage caused by her scarf tightening as she fell.

But just two days later, they realised they had made a huge mistake. The post mortem showed the popular former postmistress had been brutally stabbed to death with repeated strikes to her throat by a long-bladed knife.

By then, vital forensic evidence had been lost by emergency services and family touching objects at the crime scene and cleaning up.

“If you ‘lose a scene’ for a couple of days, as happened in 2013, you can lose some key evidence, and it’s difficult,” Det Supt Iain Moore, who led the cold case team, tells The Sun.

“It’s what is called the Golden Hour, which is the time immediately after the offence, where the evidence is rich.

“Forensic testing was still done back on the scene on the Tuesday after the murder but we just didn’t get a result back then. Whether or not we would have done, if the scene hadn’t been contaminated, is the million-dollar question.”

A police investigation threw up a list of suspects but, without the lost evidence, nothing could be proved against any of them.



Her killer walked free for 11 years until the case was re-opened in 2023 when advances in DNA technology, along with a re-examining of old interviews and fresh ones, eventually led the cold case team to a trusted neighbour.

A two-part Channel 4 special of 24 Hours in Police Custody, follows the dogged work of detectives who finally got justice for Una and her family.

“The guilty verdict was massive for the family,” says Iain. “They’re such a lovely family. They were hugely respectful to the team throughout the whole case, even taking into account the mistakes made in 2013.



“We were surprised at the decision, on the day. It was a collective one. There weren’t just police officers on the scene, there were paramedics and fire officers. Their hypothesis was that it was a non-suspicious death.

“Hindsight is a wonderful thing, but it’s just difficult to see how they came to that conclusion. However, that said, they did gain some crucial evidence at the time. So, whilst there were mistakes, there were some positives that came out of it as well.”

Judith and her husband John found Una lying dead in a pool of blood, on Sunday, 13 January, 2013, with her clothes burnt.

The curtains were still pulled and her body had been lying there since the previous evening.

They told police that it was odd there was no money in her purse because she regularly drew out a few hundred pounds to pay for odd jobs around the house or even just to bung a few quid to people who had done favours for her.



When the murder investigation belatedly got underway, a few names kept being bandied around, within the close-knit community, as Una’s likely murderers.

It was said that Damon Loates and Mark Coleman tried to steal her money and stabbed her and set her on fire. She had fallen out with her gardener over a tree that was getting cut down.

David Newton, who lived just around the corner, was volatile when drunk and was known to set fire to people’s bins and fences. And even Una’s best friend, Derek Mason, who was left £25,000 in her will, was a suspect because he benefitted financially.



In 2013, forensic scientists took two samples from Una’s fingernails. Her right hand was clenched and lying under her body, so it was protected from any burning. Advances in DNA technology were now to prove crucial.

Iain’s colleague, Detective Inspector Lee Martin Lee, visited the forensic lab where the nails and some of her clothing had been kept.

“Within DNA testing there is a profile known as Y-STR which is the male gene,” Lee explains. “That technique is getting stronger and stronger as the years move on. It can assist with pointing towards a certain bloodline.”

Forensics found a Y-STR result under Una’s fingernails which gave them a positive match to an original suspect – David Newton.



Now, all of Newton’s male relatives needed to be swabbed for DNA, as they shared the same Y-STR and to be eliminated from the enquiries. This was carried out and all of them made statements to say that they had not been in the vicinity of the crime scene at the time of the murder.

But this DNA evidence was not going to be enough for the team to be able to get a prosecution against David Newton. They also needed to build a strong circumstantial case.

Several of Newton’s family painted a dark picture of him. His daughter told detectives she didn’t like the way her dad treated her mum, Janet, throughout her life and added that her dad had ruined her childhood.

Once Janet passed away she told her father that she doubted she would ever see him again.

His brother-in-law recalled Newton hitting Janet and leaving a large bruise over her eye.



Iain and Lee re-watched a 2013 police interview with Janet, where she said her husband was an alcoholic. She also remarked that he had once gone to a locksmith for Una Crown, for new keys, because her back door lock was damaged.

Had he got an extra door key cut for himself so that he could simply let himself on that fateful day?

In his original 2013 interview, David Newton said his usual routine on a Saturday was to go to the ex-services club to play snooker. When asked if he went there again after Una was murdered, he replied, “No, I don’t think so. I didn’t have any money.”

A look back at CCTV footage from the service men’s club on Sunday 13th, the day Una was found dead, shows Newton at the bar, his snooker cue resting on the wall, taking out a large wad of notes from his wallet – unusual for somebody largely on benefits.



The following day he is seen depositing money in his bank. When questioned at the time how he came about suddenly being flush with money, he said his wife had given it to him. But, in her police interview in 2013, she denied that she had.

As well as being an aggressive alcoholic and arsonist, Newton was a voyeur, according to some.

One neighbour told police how he had just turned up at her house one day and she said she was getting ready to go out. Turning away to her bedroom, she walked off, telling him to let himself out. But the next minute, he was standing by her bedroom door, watching her in her underwear.

With their case against Newton building, officers re-arrested him.



During his new interview, Newton, then 69, replied “no comment” to everything but some key questions and comments clearly make him uncomfortable.

He is told that his neighbour, Jackie Henderson, gave a statement to say that at 8.30pm on the night of Una’s murder, she had just got back from shopping and put her bags down on the path and Newton had fallen over them. She said he appeared drunk. Newton is asked, “Was that erratic behaviour down to the fact that you had just come from Una’s bungalow, having murdered her, in a drunken state?

“Eight people from your male lineage have all given statements to say they were not in the vicinity of Una’s bungalow from 12 January 2013. The only person from the male lineage who was seen, 25 metres from Una’s property, was you, on the night she was murdered.”

Now, with enough to prosecute, David Newton was finally brought to trial and on 13 February 2025, he was found guilty of the murder of Una Crown and given a life sentence.

“I thought we had a really good case but that the problem we had was in the jury hearing about the mistakes that were made back in 2013,” says Iain.



“The jury was out for nearly 29 hours. It was really stressful, because that’s a long time. Newton remained emotionless throughout the trial and his sentence.

“It was a hugely emotional moment for the family and for me when the verdict came in. It was 11 years of waiting and one of my proudest days in policing.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Everyone in the force knew about this case because justice had not been done for Una. Now it has. And her family were, at last, allowed to move on with their grieving process.”

24 Hours in Police Custody: The Cold Case Murder, airs on Channel 4, on Monday 13 April and Tuesday 14 April.

News.title: All the Tube strike dates confirmed so far as 12 DAYS of chaos to hit entire network – starting next week
News.content:
COMMUTERS will face 12 days of travel chaos with Tube strikes expected to hit the entire network from next week.

A series of strikes are due to take place over the next three months, wreaking havoc on the London Underground.



The strikes, which will last for 24 hour periods, are a response to disputes over hours, the Rail, Maritime and Transport (RMT) Union announced.



The disruption follows the introduction of a compressed four-day working week for tube drivers, according to the RMT Union.

Union members have cited concerns relating to shift lengths, unacceptable working time arrangements, transfer and allocation processes, and the potential impact on fatigue and safety.

Industrial action was due to take place in March but was suspended after progress in talks with Transport for London.

RMT confirmed around 1,800 of its members were involved in the dispute.

Now, strikes are set to go ahead on twelve separate days spread over the course of April, May and June.

They will run over a 24-hour period from midday to midday the following day.

However, disruption is expected to continue into the afternoons and evenings on those days.

The tube strikes are scheduled to take place on the following dates:



21–22 April (12:00pm Tuesday to 11:59am Wednesday)

23–24 April (12:00pm Thursday to 11:59am Friday)

19–20 May (12:00pm Tuesday to 11:59am Wednesday)

21–22 May (12:00pm Thursday to 11:59am Friday)

16-17 June (12:00pm Tuesday to 11:59am Wednesday)

18-19 June (12:00pm Thursday to 11:59am Friday)

And while reduced services will be run, the strikes are expected to disrupt the entirety of the Tube network.

The Elizabeth line and London Overground are not expected to be directly impacted, though both will be busier than usual if the strikes go ahead.

When the Tube is down, bus and National Rail services generally offer alternative routes across the city.

E-bike hire schemes proved particularly popular during the strikes in September 2025.

News.title: I cheated death three times surviving poisoning, tsunami terror and a horror smash… doctors are shocked I’m alive
News.content:
MOST people would feel lucky to survive one near death experience – but somehow Soulla Demetriou has beaten extraordinary odds three times.

And now the 46-year-old admits: “I don’t know how many lives I have left.”



Revealing how she miraculously survived a string of terrifying experiences, Soulla, who now lives in Ibiza, told The Sun: “I have had quite a few traumatic experiences in my life. It’s like a horror film that keeps playing in my mind.”

As a child growing up in Surrey her entire family was almost wiped out by toxic carbon monoxide poisoning which was only discovered when they all fell dangerously ill on the same night.

Soulla was just 11 years old when her baby sister Sophia started having seizures.



Within hours her mother Ann became temporarily paralysed while Soulla, disorientated and suffering crippling headaches, collapsed and tumbled down the stairs.

And when they all arrived at hospital in an ambulance together on that fateful night, doctors were astounded that any of them were still alive given their oxygen levels had plummeted so alarmingly low.

“In our family home for months, actually possibly even years, in retrospect, we had been suffering different health problems, like very severe headaches,” recalled Soulla.

“One of my sisters was hospitalised with random symptoms of nausea, fainting, dizziness, and then my little sister who is 11 years younger than me, started having seizures when she was a baby.

“Over a period of about six months, she always had them very early in the morning.



“And so the doctors were wondering, is it epilepsy? My parents were trying to decide whether they had to give her medication which, as far as I’m aware, is not a decision to take lightly.

“She was taken to hospital a few times and, on one of the occasions when my little sister had a seizure, my parents actually said, ‘Can you test for carbon monoxide?’

“But there was a blood test that went missing and, unfortunately, carbon monoxide goes out of your blood stream very quickly so by the time they realised they hadn’t got the blood, it was too late to test. The next time she had a seizure was when all our levels were dangerously high.

“Our oxygen was so low.”

Although she is one of four daughters, only Soulla and Sophia were at home with their parents William and Ann on the night of the near-fatal incident. Fortunately, the older two girls were away studying.



She added: “Sophia’s bedroom was above the boiler room, and one night she had a massive seizure that woke us all up.

“And then it all went a bit crazy, because my mum was left temporarily paralysed, because her carbon monoxide levels were so high. I had a room in the attic and I fell down the stairs and cracked my skull and passed out.

I don’t know how many lives I have left at this point, but if we’re going on cat lives, I think I should start taking care Soulla Demetriou

“My dad dragged us all out of the house and called an ambulance. At this point, because the whole family was sick, he was fairly sure, without knowing 100 per cent, that we were being poisoned. Something’s happening.

“We were all taken to hospital together and they didn’t really know what to do with us at the time, because they don’t normally have people come in with that level of carbon monoxide poisoning.



“We were in hospital on oxygen for 48 hours, because there’s not much else they could do.

“My dad was also a heavy smoker but I think the adrenaline kept him alive so he could get us all out of the house. My little sister saved our lives by waking us up by having a seizure.

“We were extremely, extremely lucky, because with that much carbon monoxide, most people would have just died in their sleep.

“We were moments away from death, they said to us.



“It was a very traumatic experience, and it was probably my first experience of PTSD.

“But at the time, there wasn’t really any treatment, not through anyone’s fault. We just survived it and that felt like a miracle. We were very grateful to be alive but then we carried on with our lives.

“Within a few years I was having a lot of anxiety. That sense of inner safety was really ruptured and I’d have flashbacks of that moment when my sister was unconscious for a really long time while we waited for the ambulance – not knowing if she was dead or alive.”

Holiday terror

Years later the closely-bonded family shared a trip of a lifetime to Sri Lanka but during their 2004 holiday the deadly Boxing Day tsunami struck, killing more than 31,000 people.

Soulla, who had been having therapy for panic attacks, was left stranded on the third floor of their hotel while William was miles out to sea on a deep sea fishing trip with her then boyfriend and her older sister’s partners.



For hours, as buildings collapsed around them, they had no idea if the four men were dead or alive.

She said: “Again, it’s a kind of double-edged experience of being very lucky but also still going through an extremely challenging, terrifying experience.

“At first we didn’t really understand what was going on. We were in the restaurant on the third floor but then the water started rising to our level and people on surfboards were jumping inside, to get out of the water.



“There was a phone blackout. There was this sense of terror, and no idea what’s going to happen next.

“When it’s nature, it’s so much bigger than you and we were like sitting ducks with no idea if the wave would come back. We just had to wait.

“We couldn’t get hold of my dad all day, and there was nothing we could do. It was just shock and utter terror, and this panic.

My little sister asked me, ‘Are we just very unlucky?’ But I think we are really lucky actually because we keep surviving things that other people haven’t Soulla Demetriou

“Obviously I was very distressed about not seeing my partner and just feeling so helpless.

“I remember going down to the hotel manager, and everyone’s panicking, but just after sunset suddenly there they were, covered in mud but alive, and that, again, was like a miracle.



“They’d been lucky, because no fish had bitten – we now know that was because of the tsunami – and so they had turned to sail further out.

“Of course, it was kind of a race against the wave, against being swallowed back into the depth of the sea but being further away from the shore was what saved them.”

Even after the family was reunited they struggled to celebrate amid the devastation.



Soulla added: “There was so much gratitude, but there was death everywhere. We wanted to leave, but there were people who had lost everything.

“It was so traumatic, we felt so helpless. We bought sacks of rice and baby bottles, and took them to the camps, but there were just piles of bodies and people wearing rescue blankets.

“When we did eventually get on a plane, it was full of empty seats.

“It was very palpable, the enormous privilege of being able to leave alive, while all these people were devastated by trauma and loss.”



Days later, Soulla was back at her advertising job in London, but unable to focus.

She said: “We had our Monday status meeting and I was looking around thinking this makes no sense, this does not matter. And that really fuelled me to make a change in my life.”

Soulla ditched the corporate world and went travelling around South America and South East Asia, retrained as a yoga teacher and is now running retreats helping people change how they live, think and feel.



She eventually settled in Ibiza but two years ago near-tragedy struck yet again.

“I was kite surfing when a gust of wind picked up very suddenly and lifted me up and smashed me into a variety of very hard things before throwing me into a building, and then I dropped, like a stone to the ground,” she added.

“I had internal organ damage and was in hospital for a month.

“Again, I had a diagnosis of PTSD from that. But I think what was really interesting to me was that I was better resourced this time. Even as I was waiting for the ambulance to arrive, I was thinking, ‘Okay what are the tools I need?’

“Because I didn’t know at that point how serious the injuries were. I couldn’t breathe, I was in agony, I had a bad head injury, neck injury, spine and ribs.



“My little sister asked me, ‘Are we just very unlucky?’ But I think we are really, really lucky actually because we keep surviving things that other people haven’t.

“I don’t know how many lives I have left at this point, but if we’re going on cat lives, I think I should start taking care!”

Now Soulla has published an inspiring new book called You Have Always Been Enough: A Healing Guide to Self-Love and Inner Freedom which reflects what she has learnt along the way.



She explained: “I wouldn’t say there’s one specific moment that led to the book, it has been very much informed by my own personal journey – a culmination of many different moments which led to a lot of pain, suffering and emotional challenges in my life.”

You Have Always Been Enough by Soulla Demetriou is available from Harper Collins now £16.99.

News.title: Shane Warne's son blames Covid vaccine for Australian cricket icon's death
News.content:
Shane Warne's son blames Covid vaccine for Australian cricket icon's death

Australian cricket legend Shane Warne died in March 2022 from a heart attack while on holiday in Thailand and his son Jackson has given his perspective on the tragedy

View 2 Images Shane Warne (Image: Daniel Pockett)

Shane Warne's son believes the Covid-19 vaccine contributed to his death from a heart attack at the age of 52. Warne passed away in March 2022 while on holiday in Thailand.

‌



A post-mortem showed no signs of foul play and concluded he died of died of a "congenital disease". The former Australian cricket star was found unresponsive in a villa on Koh Samui island and efforts to resuscitate him were unsuccessful.

‌



A Thai police spokesman said in a statement at the time: "Investigators received an autopsy report today in which a forensic doctor concludes the death was due to natural causes."

‌



A senior police officer who attended the scene later said that Kamagra, a super strength sex drug known as 'Viagra jelly', was found by his body but was removed due to orders from above.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! All the best sports news and much more on our dedicated Facebook page

Rory McIlroy responds to 'unfair' accusations after beating Scottie Scheffler to Masters READ MORE :

Colchester United issue statement after John Terry takeover reports READ MORE :

Jackson Warne, 26, has now explained his theory about his dad's death. Asked on the 2 Worlds Collide Podcast if the Covid-19 vaccine killed the cricket legend, he replied: "I definitely think that it was involved. I don't even think saying that is controversial anymore. Even if dad had underlying health issues, I think this brought it straight to the surface.

‌



"My first impression, as soon as I hung up the phone, I instantly blamed the government. I instantly blamed Covid and the vaccine. Doing things like the state memorial, where that's funded by Vic Gov and the MCG and there has to be certain due diligence and people in the crowds have to get photos and all that stuff, I felt really uncomfortable.

"At the state memorial, I nearly said I blame the government and Covid, but I didn't. It was probably smart I didn't - I'd be in a very different position if I did. But that was how I felt. Even the last three or four years, I have not changed my tune.

View 2 Images Jackson Warne has a theory about his father's death (Image: Philip Brown/Getty Images)

‌



"At the end of the day, we'll never know. The autopsy is online. I know what happened to him. Dad, at the time, was healthy, he was happy. He looked the best he had in a while. Yes, he smoked and drank, but how many more people in their 80s and 90s still smoke and drink a lot more than dad?

"Yes, a lot of people were dying of heart attacks before. But dad was ok, I think he might have got three or four [vaccine jabs], he didn't want to get them, he was forced to get them for work.

"He was forced to get them like everybody else. Dad wasn't the only person. When dad passed, he was probably the most famous Australian that people could go, 'yep, that's Covid,' but I try not to think about it too much because all that does is fester into anger. That anger is not good for anybody."

Article continues below

He added: "If something comes out like this again, at least we're more awake, at least we're more aware. If dad had underlying health issues, maybe he was going to have a heart attack at 65, 70, but I think this just brought it all to the surface."

News.title: Border chaos explained - why Easyjet passengers missed flight as new travel rules start
News.content:
Border chaos explained - why Easyjet passengers missed flight as new travel rules start

With EasyJet passengers missing flights, and tourists with other airlines left affected too, the Mirror can explain more about the rules that have come into affected at European Union nations

View 4 Images Chaos at Milan Linate airport on Sunday (Image: Emily_Benn20/X)

Brits have been plunged into travel chaos after long delays due to new EU border rules had led to some passengers missing their flights home and ending up stranded abroad.

‌



Around 100 EasyJet passengers were left behind when a flight from Milan's Linate airport to Manchester left travellers behind who were stuck in massive lines, on Sunday. The new European Entry/Exit System (EES) was fully rolled out across the EU on Friday and it requires people from third-party countries, including the UK, to go through biometric and facial recognition checks.

‌



Huge lines hit major airports in several cities, including Paris, Lisbon and Milan, as desperate travellers were forced to wait to clear immigration.

‌



Some stranded passengers claimed people were vomiting and passing out in the huge queues at Milan's Linate airport, on Sunday, as they also dealt with a heatwave.

View 4 Images EasyJet said the situation was 'outside of our control' (Image: X)

What is the EES?

The EU's Entry/Exit System started on October 12, 2025, but it was rolled out fully on Friday, April 10. It is a new digital border system for people from third-party countries, including the UK, entering the Schengen area.

‌



This new system has replaced the old method of officials manually stamping passports when people arrive into the Schengen area.

What will the new process look like for Brits?

British travellers could now be asked to create a digital record at the port or airport on arrival, on their first visit to a Schengen area country after this new system. People no not have to fill anything out before they travel and the EES registration is free of charge.

Travellers could be asked to have a photo taken at a dedicated booth and submit their fingerprints. People could also be asked to provide fingerprints or a photo when they leave the Schengen area.

‌



The government noted that the EES may take "each passenger a few extra minutes to complete", but once done, the EES record is valid for three years.

View 4 Images Delays at Brussels Airport amid the full Entry/Exit System (EES) rollout (Image: @PolarFish41/X)

What issues have travellers faced so far?

One Brit revealed she was among the 100 people desperate to get home after the EasyJet flight took off from Milan and abandoned them. Carol Boon, 59, speaking to the BBC, said she had been away for a hen do but was left stuck in a "very stressful" situation at the airport with "people arguing, someone fainted, someone was sick".

‌



Another traveller, Max Hume, from Leeds, told the BBC that he spent a staggering £1,800 to get back home as soon as possible and travelled through Luxembourg.

EasyJet told The Mirror that the ordeal was "outside of our control" and said it held the flight for nearly an hour, adding: "These delays are unacceptable and so we continue to urge border authorities to ensure they make full and effective use of the permitted flexibilities for as long as needed so our customers' travel plans are not impacted.

View 4 Images Some passengers complained about the compensation they received after the travel chaos (Image: X)

‌



"Should a customer miss their flight due to EES delays they are offered free flight transfers on a later easyJet flight. For customers who book on other airlines they will need to contact their travel insurance to make a claim."

Another passenger slammed EasyJet for the ordeal and claimed she was only offered £12.25 in compensation from the airline. Speaking to the BBC, the 17-year-old student, from Oldham, Greater Manchester, said she was forced to wait 20 hours in the airport with her boyfriend until they could get a flight the next day.

Kiera said these new flights would set her mum back £520 and they were going to Gatwick instead of Manchester. The student added that the couple got to the airport hours ahead of their flight but still didn't make it on. She said: "We got here at seven-thirty for our flight at eleven so were super early. We got to Border Control and it was a massive queue of people."

Article continues below

Jet2 has issued a fresh alert to passengers at Faro Airport, in Portugal, after reports of "congestion" through the site. In response to a passenger's post online, a spokesperson for the airport said "the queues are completely out of our control", adding: "We kindly recommend customers arrive to the airport as early as possible, to allow plenty of time to make it through."

A spokesperson for ABTA, the association of travel agents and tour operators, says: "We’re advising passengers to go straight to passport control as soon as you have gone through check-in and security; that way you get the EES checks out of the way as early as possible.

"We’re also advising passengers to follow their transport provider's advice on when to arrive at airports/ports etc. If flying, the usual rule is to arrive at the airport for a flight from Europe at least two hours before, so we’d encourage people to apply that as a minimum, but to also check with their airline and airport."

News.title: Should balaclavas be banned in the UK? Take our poll and have your say
News.content:
Should balaclavas be banned in the UK? Take our poll and have your say

Amy Hodson-Ridgway, a mum from Manchester, has launched a petition to ban balaclavas after a masked gang ploughed into her eight-year-old son, leaving him with several injuries

View 3 Images Ethan Hodson-Ridgway after he was knocked over by a masked gang on E-bikes (Image: Amy Ridgway / SWNS)

The growing calls to ban balaclavas have been joined by a mother whose son, 8, was left "traumatised" when a gang on E-bikes ran him over.

‌



Ethan Hodson-Ridgway flew 10ft into the air after two masked thugs hit into the little boy outside his home, in Manchester, in December. The eight-year-old was left with shocking injuries, including a broken tibia and fibula in his left leg, a collapsed lung and sustained a gash to his head.

‌



Ethan's mum Amy Hodson-Ridgway, 34, has joined calls for the government to implement a balaclava ban. Amy, in her campaigns, has claimed these sorts of masks "provide anonymity to countless individuals committing crimes".

‌



The mum created a Change.org petition called "ban balaclavas to make our streets safer" and has amassed more than 50,000 signatures so far. Have your say with our poll below and post a comment in the section below.

Amy said despite handing over footage of the horror incident to the police, the cops were unable to identify the suspects because their identities were hidden. The case was then closed just three weeks later.

‌



There are currently no laws outlawing the wearing of balaclavas, though local councils can use Public Space Protection Orders (PSPOs) to allow police to issue fines to those who refuse to remove face coverings.

3 View 3 Images The eight-year-old in hospital (Image: Amy Ridgway / SWNS) 3 View 3 Images Mum Amy said balaclavas 'provide anonymity to countless individuals committing crimes' (Image: Amy Ridgway / SWNS)

Article continues below

Police also have powers to ask people to remove face coverings at protests, and building owners can ask people to leave their premises if wearing them on private land.

Amy said: "This single piece of clothing has turned our community into a breeding ground for lawlessness and fear. They embolden criminals, from petty thieves to dangerous drivers, allowing them to evade accountability."

There was concern youths had attempted to hide their identities by wearing balaclavas and other coverings when they ran riot in Clapham in south London, Birmingham city centre and other places this month.

News.title: Keir Starmer sends urgent warning to Israel over Lebanon strikes as pressure mounts
News.content:
Keir Starmer sends urgent warning to Israel over Lebanon strikes as pressure mounts

Keir Starmer has ramped up pressure on Israel to stop its strikes on Lebanon as he warned of a "devastating" crisis in the country as he gave a statement to MPs

View 4 Images Keir Starmer has ramped up pressure on Israel to stop its strikes on Lebanon as he warned of a "devastating" crisis in the country (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Keir Starmer has ramped up pressure on Israel to stop its strikes on Lebanon as he warned of a "devastating" crisis in the country.

‌



The Prime Minister said the Middle East "remains on the edge" as a ceasefire brokered by the US, Israel and Iran is "highly fragile". He reiterated his demands for Lebanon to be "urgently" included in the agreement.

‌



And Mr Starmer slapped down Donald Trump's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz saying the UK wants the vital shipping route to be "open, not shut". He said the UK is "not supporting the blockade" and repeated his position that the UK "is not getting dragged into" the Iran war.

‌



In a statement lasting nearly two hours in Parliament, the PM told the Commons the UK must meet the challenge of the volatile world "calmly but with strength".

He said the Strait has been "shamefully exploited by Iran" during the conflict and said Gulf leaders that he met last week were "crystal clear that freedom of navigation is vital and must be restored".

View 4 Images The PM said the Middle East "remains on the edge" as a ceasefire brokered by the US, Israel and Iran is "highly fragile" (Image: PRU/AFP via Getty Images)

‌



He told MPs: “Whilst the ceasefire between the US, Israel and Iran is undeniably welcome, it is also highly fragile. The region remains on edge, and a lot of work is required to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, to de-escalate the situation, leading to a sustainable ceasefire.

“In pursuit of that goal, we call for Lebanon to be included urgently in the ceasefire. Diplomacy is the right path, and I welcome the talks taking place this week. Hezbollah must disarm, but I’m equally clear Israel’s strikes are wrong. They are having devastating humanitarian consequences and pushing Lebanon into a crisis.”

The PM's cool-headedness was contrasted by erratic Mr Trump's continued hostile and violent threats in the region.

‌



The US President on Monday afternoon began his own blockade of Iranian ports, deepening the global economic impact from the Middle East crisis.

In an extraordinary showdown, Mr Trump warned Iranian naval ships approaching the US blockade will be “eliminated” using the same “quick and brutal” method to destroy drug dealers’ boats.

A notice to mariners issued by the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency, which monitors maritime security, said the restrictions included "the entirety of the Iranian coastline, including ports and energy infrastructure."

‌



View 4 Images The US President on Monday afternoon began his own blockade of Iranian ports (Image: AP)

In a post on his Truth Social platform, the US president wrote: “Iran’s Navy is laying at the bottom of the sea, completely obliterated – 158 ships. What we have not hit are their small number of, what they call, ‘fast attack ships,’ because we did not consider them much of a threat. Warning: If any of these ships come anywhere close to our BLOCKADE, they will be immediately ELIMINATED, using the same system of kill that we use against the drug dealers on boats at Sea. “It is quick and brutal. PS 98.2% of Drugs coming into the US by Ocean or Sea have STOPPED! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DJT”.

Ebrahim Rezaei, a spokesperson for the Iranian parliament's National Security Commission, dismissed US warnings of a potential blockade as "more bluffing than reality," while warning that Tehran was prepared to respond if the situation escalates militarily.

‌



Asked whether the UK will support a US military blockade - for instance with British minesweepers in the region - Mr Starmer told BBC Radio 5: "We're not supporting the blockade."

He said any UK diplomatic or political efforts, as well as minesweeping capabilities in the region, are "all focused from our point of view on getting the Straits fully open". He added: "The reason for that is because that's the way we get energy prices down as quickly as possible.

View 4 Images The UK and France will co-host a summit this week "to drive forward the international effort" to end the conflict and unblock the Strait (Image: AP)

‌



The UK and France will co-host a summit this week "to drive forward the international effort" to end the conflict and unblock the Strait.

The PM has repeatedly said full freedom of navigation must be restored on the shipping route with no conditions or tolls.

Iran's chokehold on the vital shipping lane, which transports around a fifth of the world's oil and gas, has sent gas prices spiralling. Oil prices spiked back to more than 100 US dollars (£74) a barrel after US peace talks with Iran broke down and the US president made his belligerent threat to prevent ships leaving from this afternoon.

‌



The war could leave the average UK household £480 worse off over the current financial year than if the conflict had not happened, the Resolution Foundation think tank has warned.

In the Commons, MPs challenged Mr Starmer on what action the UK is taking to de-escalate the situation, including in Lebanon.

Emily Thornberry, chair of the foreign affairs' committee, told the Prime Minister her "blood ran cold" over Israel's threat to follow "the model in Gaza" in Lebanon as she asked what the UK is doing to ensure a ceasefire in Lebanon.

‌



Lebanese, Israeli and US officials are due to hold talks in Washington on Tuesday. Confusion erupted last week after Iran insisted Lebanon had been included in a ceasefire agreement, while the US and Israel said it was not.

Elsewhere, Mr Starmer insisted the UK's defence investment plan was being finalised after long delays.

He told MPs: "It's really important that we don't make the mistakes that the last government made. We inherited plans which were unfunded and not deliverable and it's really important, therefore, that our plan is robust. We're finalising it, but it will be a robust plan that serves for the future of defence and protection of this country."

Article continues below

Deputy PM David Lammy has travelled to the US where he was on Monday expected to meet US Vice President JD Vance and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Rachel Reeves will on travel to Washington DC on Tuesday to discuss the economic impact of the Middle East crisis at a crunch summit.

News.title: 'I live in Southport and there's a tragic detail after murders that people forget'
News.content:
EXCLUSIVE: 'I live in Southport and there's a tragic detail after murders that people forget'

As the first phase of the Southport Inquiry report is published, the Mirror speaks to members of a community which has rallied in the face of unimaginable tragedy

View 12 Images Axel Rudakubana was jailed for life for the heinous murders (Image: PA)

Southport locals are still reeling from Axel Rudakubana's heinous child murders in a town that prides itself on being a safe haven for families.

‌



Like far too many, Andrew Brown remembers the events of July 29, 2024, all too well. After a fairly dismal summer, his seaside hometown of Southport had exploded in glorious sunshine.

‌



Holidaymakers had poured into the Merseyside town, with its quaint Victorian architecture and famous pleasure pier, taking boats out on the lake and riding the carousel.

‌



Dad-of-two Andrew had been over in the pretty village of Ainsdale, some three miles from the centre, attending the North West in Bloom Awards. The floral displays were spectacular that year, and Andrew remembers how "stunning" everything looked.

Speaking with the Mirror, Andrew recalled: "Loads of families, loads of people having fun and, you thought, 'Wow Southport's looking really good'." It was then that the messages began to trickle through. Something had happened on Hart Street.

Southport killer parents' warped life tormented by son and forced into hiding READ MORE :

View 12 Images July 29, 2024 began with sunshine and joy, and ended in tragedy (Image: STEVE ALLEN)

‌



Talk of a police presence in the suburban Meols Cop area quickly escalated into something far more devastating. Andrew, who runs the positive community news website, Stand Up for Southport, remembered: "Then all the rumours started, and people sent a message through saying somebody's died, somebody's been attacked." Like many others, Andrew was left scrambling to find out information and clarity, separating the facts from the "complete rubbish" that was cropping up on social media.

In a few short hours, what should have been an idyllic summer's day descended into one of the most tragic moments in Southport's history. When the truth emerged, it would leave a nation sickened. Axel Rudakubana, a 17-year-old whose behaviour had sparked serious concerns at his former school, had stormed a Taylor Swift-themed dance class at The Hart Space shortly before midday, wielding a knife he'd purchased on Amazon.

Rudakubana, who had long harboured an obsession with extreme violence, attacked the group of 25 youngsters, killing Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine; Bebe King, six; and Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven. It later emerged that the warped teenager had been reported to the government's Prevent counter-extremism scheme at least three times before the attack, but each time it was determined he wasn't a high enough risk.

‌



View 12 Images The families of the three little girls continue to honour their lives through charitable endeavours (Image: PA)

For Southport-born Andrew, the contrast between the scenes of horror and the "amazing town" couldn't be starker. He reflected: "It just seemed unreal. I mean, Southport's a beautiful, friendly, welcoming seaside town. It's a town with a real sense of community, a real sense of togetherness.

"I was living in Liverpool, met my wife, got married, and we moved to Southport to raise a family because it's a family place. So for something like this to happen, it's still shocking now. It's shocking to happen anywhere in the world and to happen here, because this is a place where families come for happy memories, and it just seemed so appalling and gruesome and tragic."

‌



Today, an inquiry into the attack listed five major areas of systemic failure across multiple agencies, which could have stopped Rudakubana, concluding that the murders had been "foreseeable and avoidable". Delivering phase one of his inquiry at Liverpool Town Hall, inquiry chairman Sir Adrian Fulford began by describing the attack as one of "unparalleled cruelty", of which "nothing matching the extreme and very particular depravity" has occurred in modern-day Britain.

View 12 Images Rudakubana's parents have been subject to criticism in the report (Image: PA)

Outlining how the killer "perpetrated a chilling and carefully planned assault", Sir Adrian said: "He travelled by taxi to a Taylor Swift-themed dance and yoga event, where he killed and inflicted devastating injuries on as many children as he was able. He did not hesitate, in the process, to assault and gravely injure two adults in his path. AR had earlier selected this particular venue as his target, and I am confident that from the advertising for this event on social media, he was fully aware that those attending would be very young girls, along with the two female organisers."

‌



He added: "What we know, instead, is that from his early teens he had become ever more fixated on extreme violence. I have no doubt that this disturbing preoccupation had been fed during the many years when, wholly unsupervised and lacking any parental controls, he spent the majority of his waking hours online. The strong indications are that he fuelled his perversely violent fixation by viewing a wide range of deeply inappropriate and disturbing subjects that are all too available on the internet.

"It is no coincidence that one of the last things he did before he left his family's home to commit these cruel offences was to locate a graphic and simply appalling video on X (formerly known as Twitter) of a knife attack on Bishop Emmanuel in Australia. This was, beyond doubt, to strengthen his resolve to carry through with his cowardly and murderous plan."

View 12 Images Locals were devastated that this crime could occur in such a 'beautiful, friendly, welcoming seaside town' (Image: STEVE ALLEN)

‌



Three days before the dammning report was released, The Mirror visited Southport and was struck by how lovely the town centre looks in the sunshine. The tree-lined Lord Street, with its pretty glazed canopies, feels tailor-made for relaxed springtime strolls, bringing a charming Parisian feel to Merseyside. The fountains of the tranquil landscaped gardens sparkle in the April sunlight, and more than one admiring tourist stops to take a picture of the Palladian-style town hall, framed by a dreamy blue sky.

This is a place of ice creams and florists, of the scent of coffee drifting delicately from inviting cafes. Generations of Brits have enjoyed holidays and day trips here, and there's no sense of a dark shadow looming over the leafy boulevards. Proud locals have worked extraordinarily hard over the past two years to ensure Southport retains its legacy of sunny friendliness, against seemingly impossible odds. It didn't initially seem that this could be the case.

Just 24 hours after the tragedy, two local women organised a vigil in the picturesque town hall gardens. It's a detail that, unfortunately, often gets lost in the chaos that was unfolding elsewhere. Andrew, who was in attendance at the vigil, said: "I think it was one of the most emotional things I've ever been to. You had so many families there and people bringing flowers and people hugging each other, and He had a chaplain, Reverend Martin Evans from the local hospital, who stood up and must have been so difficult for him to speak, but he spoke to the crowd, and there was a time for everybody coming together."

‌



View 12 Images The heartfelt vigil held in the wake of the tragedy sadly often gets forgotten due to the riots which followed (Image: STEVE ALLEN)

While still at the heartfelt vigil, Andrew received a phone call from somebody telling him to get away from town, warning that there was a riot underway. At first, he assumed they must have been mistaken. Andrew told us: "I said, 'No, you've got that wrong, it's a vigil, there is nothing happening. No, no, there's no riot here'." It was then that he learned that there was indeed a riot unfolding outside the mosque, situated around one mile away from where locals had gathered in the Town Hall Gardens.

Misinformation and false allegations regarding the perpetrator had spread like wildfire over social media, leading to far-right thugs taking to the streets with yet more mindless violence, piling on the heartache for locals who had already suffered so much.

‌



Andrew said: "I think it was just shocking because people in Southport came together with compassion, and their only feeling was for their families affected and for the victims, and it just seemed completely out of place that other people's reaction, other people coming in and their feeling wasn't compassion towards the families. It was hatred. And that wasn't what people in Southport were feeling at the time."

View 12 Images Rampaging protestors torched vehicles and hurled bricks during the riots (Image: Getty Images)

Mere hours after the attack, an X account known as 'Europe Invasion' falsely posted that the then-unnamed suspect was 'a Muslim immigrant', despite the official police report asserting that the person in custody had been born in Cardiff, Wales. Close to four million users saw this post, and the dangerous information continued to spread. Posts wrongly named the killer as an individual called 'Ali-Al-Shakati', falsely claimed to be an asylum seeker who'd travelled to the UK by boat the year before.

‌



By 10 pm that evening, posts containing the false name and details had garnered more than six million impressions, leading to far higher engagement on posts which linked Southport with search terms including 'muslim', 'islam' and 'asylum'. All the while, artificial intelligence had been used to create fake images depicting Muslims wielding knives, clocking up thousands of shares.

Merseyside Police reported at the time that 53 officers were injured in the Southport riots, with eight having sustained serious injuries, as the hundreds-strong crowd descended. The force told of how offenders destroyed garden walls, using bricks as missiles to lob at officers. Cars belonging to members of the public were on fire at random, as were wheelie bins. Bricks were thrown at the local mosque, while a local convenience store was damaged. Three police dogs were also injured, with yobs attacking them wth bricks.

Andrew continued: "It's sad that the vigil has kind of been forgotten in the passage of time. And people look back and go, 'Oh, after the tragedy, there was a riot'. And to me, no, after the tragedy, there was a vigil. That's what should be remembered, but unfortunately, the riots were."

‌



View 12 Images Locals are working hard to build the community back up about the attacks (Image: STEVE ALLEN)

What also should be remembered is how, the day after the riots, well-meaning locals came out in force to help clear up the scenes of destruction, bringing along hose pipes and brushes, and even food and dog food for the set-upon officers.

This spirit of neighbourliness continued to flourish from there. The Mirror also heard from Debbie Fullwood, chairperson for the Southport Interfaith Group, a community coalition she says was "formed and grew out of the dirt and debris of the prejudiced and divisive riots."

‌



With the aim of fostering solidarity and friendship across religious groups in the area, members now meet up regularly, calmly and determinedly combating the extremist division which brought additional agony in the final weeks of that terrible summer.

View 12 Images The first phase of the Southport Inquiry Report ws published today (Image: PA)

Debbie explained: "Our group's aim is to offer hope, and our mission is to promote friendship, understanding and cooperation among our faith communities, working together for the peace, social cohesion and the well-being of the Southport area and all who live here."

‌



While the riots and the false rumours made headlines at the time, Debbie believes the furious rioters did not speak for the majority of the town. Debbie shared: "The majority internal voice in the town at the time was definitely that of peacemaker. We wanted to find the calm within the storm, unity, mutual respect and support."

Events held by the Interfaith Group include the Walk of Unity, which sees leaders from different faiths walking along together with members of the public, sharing conversation, and then lunch. It's a powerful message that others around the world could do well to note.

View 12 Images Today, the Southport Inquiry has provided some long-awaited answers (Image: STEVE ALLEN)

‌



As put movingly by Andrew: "You look around the world, and you look at Ukraine, and you look at Gaza, and you look at Iran and all the conflicts, and then you see all these religious leaders in Southport walking kind of hand in hand together, you know. Smiling and joking and sharing stories.

"And you think that's what the world should be like. So I think Southport's got a sense of togetherness that's come out of just about the worst thing that could have happened. It has got this sense of compassionate togetherness, which maybe could be a lesson to the rest of the world."

Although the attacks themselves revealed the very worst of humanity, the peaceful community-focused initiatives have proven to be a light in the darkness. Debbie said: "I do believe that out of the horrors of that summer, there are some silver linings that have come about within our community. The charities created by each of the girls' families are our inspiration."

‌



The work of the three charities has proven tireless and extraordinary, a testament to the courageous parents determined to build a lasting, far-reaching legacy for their beloved daughters. There's Alice's WonderDance, which helps support young dancers with expenses such as exams, uniforms, and equipment, with the aim of "ensuring that every child, regardless of ability, background, gender, culture, or socioeconomic status, feels welcome, valued, and able to participate fully in dance experiences."

View 12 Images Amid the sorrow, Southport locals have banded together (Image: Liverpool Echo)

Alice's father, Sergio Aguiar, will be running six of the world's major marathons this April to raise money for the organisation, including the London Marathon, which he will be running alongside Elsie's dad, David Stancombe. Meanwhile, Elsie's Story, a charitable trust focused on "memory-making days, care grants, and community-led kindness", has raised more than £1 million.

‌



At the moment, work is also underway to create Bebe's Hive, described by organisers as a "safe place where grieving children can find creativity and connection". The three families have also secured £10 million from the government to transform the town hall gardens into a creative event space for families.

According to Andrew: "They don't want a memorial, they want a place for joy and laughter and events and festivals and dancing, and they want to bring happiness to other children of the families." It's a vision that feels very much in keeping with Southport, a place of gentle yet meaningful gestures, and it's clear those in the area have been touched by such efforts.

View 12 Images Bridgette Higgins shared a photo of a "beautiful sentiment" she found attached to her gate

‌



Speaking with the Mirror, local woman Bridgette Higgins shared a photo of a "beautiful sentiment" she found attached to her gate that very day, raising awareness of Bebe's Hive. Bridgette had moved to the Southport area from Bedfordshire prior to the attack, intent on "making a new life" for herself. As she settled into her routine in the North West, she had no idea of the difficulties her new hometown was about to face.

Bridgette shared: "Living close to Churchtown Primary, the school of two of the girls, my husband and I volunteered to help tend the flowers. How do you console our elderly 'lollipop chap' (school crossing patrol) who had cheered and encouraged happy girls safely across the road every morning of their school life? Everyday folks doing everyday tasks, paralysed by grief, anger and disbelief."

At that time, Bridgette herself had been facing health problems, but the tragedy put her own issues into sharp perspective. She added, "I was midway through a course of chemotherapy. Initially, I thought chemotherapy was the worst thing that could happen until this tragedy put my six-month ordeal into perspective. I never moaned once about my treatment after this horrific event. Nothing could heal this atrocity."

Article continues below

In January 2025, Rudakubana was handed a life sentence with a minimum of 52 years behind bars. It won't be him, or the violent rioters that followed, who will be remembered by the people of Southport. And as today's report is published, locals will be looking ahead to brighter months to come, taking great, and deserved, pride in their unshakeable community spirit.

News.title: Tragedy as Tommy Verbickas dies aged just 6 after his third cancer battle
News.content:
Tragedy as Tommy Verbickas dies aged just 6 after his third cancer battle

Tommy Verbickas, from Sale, Greater Manchester, was just two years old when he was diagnosed with Wilms tumour — a form of kidney cancer — after medics found a mass

View 3 Images Tommy Verbicka has passed away after three cancer fights (Image: MEN MEDIA)

A six-year-old boy has died after his third cancer battle.

‌



Tommy Verbickas was first diagnosed with cancer in February 2022 at just two years old when doctors found a 2.3kg mass on his left kidney. Medics discovered the toddler had Wilms tumour — a form of kidney cancer — and the brave youngster had to undergo chemotherapy and surgery.

‌



The little boy, from Sale, Greater Manchester, rang the end-of-treatment bell in November 2022, before sadly relapsing twice and facing cancer for a third time. He has now passed away, his family has said.

‌



Relatives added they hope he is "flying high, dancing through the rainbows." They said: "Our special boy Tommy we hope you're flying high, dancing through the rainbows. Until we meet again our precious boy."

3 View 3 Images Tommy is pictured with his parents, who are from Sale in Greater Manchester (Image: PA Real Life) 3 View 3 Images Tommy was described as the 'most amazing, bravest and courageous little boy' (Image: PA Real Life)

‌



Earlier this week, the family posted about Tommy's condition and how sad they were that they wouldn't have more time with him. They said: "Tommy is still fighting, just as he has done for the past four years. It all feels so unbearably unfair, especially with how quickly everything is happening. I truly believed we’d have more time - time for one last trip to the beach altogether, another battle royale on his PS5, and simply for him to give his dog one more cuddle.

"Watching your precious child fade before your eyes is a pain no parent should ever have to endure. It’s the most heartbreaking kind of helplessness.He is genuinely incredible, and with every breath he takes, he keeps showing just how strong and determined he is."

In an post on April 4, Tommy's mum spoke about how the cancer in his lung had rapidly progressed and how his condition was deteriorating, calling it "the hardest thing we've ever faced," Manchester Evening News reports.

‌



Since his passing, tributes and kind words have flooded in for the "most amazing, bravest and courageous little boy" who showed "so much strength and bravery."

Karen Harrison said: "Tommy the most amazing, bravest and courageous little boy who we love so much. Words can’t describe how we feel right now.

"But we know he will be the brightest star shining in the sky tonight and always. We will never forget him and his cheeky ways and that he still called me Mrs Harrison after 4 years."

Article continues below

Another tribute said that Tommy had 'fought a fight no child ever should'. Jill Stephens said: "He fought a fight no child ever should, but boy did he fight. You gave him everything, every chance, every bit of love. We will always carry him with us, and we will now help carry you through life ahead."

Manchester United will host Leeds as they make the journey across the Pennines to reignite their famed rivalry in a Premier League clash with ramifications at both ends of the table.

Much has changed since these sides last met, with January’s reverse fixture - a 1-1 draw at Elland Road - proving the breaking point for Ruben Amorim’s ill-fated 14-month reign as United manager.

News.title: Best home security system of 2026: Top alarms tested and reviewed by an expert
News.content:
What is the best smart home security system?

SimpliSafe is currently my favourite smart home security system. It is very easy to set up and install, and there’s a wide range of optional extras to build a whole-home system. But what helps this house alarm stand out from its rivals is the option to pay £27.99 a month for professional monitoring. Since Ring and Eufy don’t offer this service in the UK, it’s something that puts Simplisafe at the top of our list. The Yale smart alarm also offers full, 24/7 professional monitoring, but at a higher monthly cost of £36 per month.

If you don’t need professional monitoring, then check out Ring alarm and the Eufy home alarm kit. Both offer excellent alarm kits that connect to their wider smart home systems comprising security cameras, video doorbells and more. I especially like how Eufy records footage locally, thus avoiding the cloud storage fees imposed by Ring. Or, if you want a security system on a budget, Blink performs well and its simple security cameras are often priced from below £30.

Finally, if you want to build a large smart home system, I recommend TP-Link Tapo, since the H500 smart HomeBase hub has Matter support that makes it compatible with a huge number of smart home devices and accessories, beyond just security products.

How to choose the best home security system for you

Most smart home security and alarm systems are designed to be installed with simple DIY skills. They connect to your router and use wireless, battery-powered sensors that attach to doors, windows and walls with included adhesive pads or screws and wall plugs. You might need a ladder and a drill to mount outdoor security cameras and sirens – and some basic electrical knowledge if hardwiring a video doorbell – but that’s as complex as it gets. After installation, the systems are usually set up using a smartphone app. Verisure is one of the few systems that requires professional installation.

The essentials

When choosing a home security system, start with the essentials. This usually includes a hub or base station that connects devices (like door sensors and motion detectors) to a smartphone app and the internet. Basic kits usually also include the aforementioned sensors and a keypad or fob for arming and disarming the system; some come with external sirens too. Additional sensors, cameras and other devices can be bought separately and added to expand your system.

Key features

Key features to look out for are battery and cellular backup, which keep the system working during a power cut or broadband blackout. Smart home compatibility can be a useful extra, where voice assistants like Siri, Alexa and Google Assistants control the alarm. If you already own connected cameras or a video doorbell, then it’s worth checking if there’s an alarm system that works with your existing devices for a more seamless installation.

Subscriptions

Costs vary depending on system size and subscription options. Some systems charge a monthly or annual subscription fee for cloud video storage; these fees also sometimes unlock extras like smarter, AI-powered person recognition for security cameras, and cellular backup.

Alarm systems from Simplisafe, Yale and Verisure charge for professional monitoring, where an agent responds to alerts and can even call the emergency services on your behalf. Professional monitoring is not available in the UK from Ring, Tapo or Eufy – but the latter two remain good options if you want to monitor things yourself, since they store camera footage locally and charge no ongoing fee.

Other smart security brands to consider

We haven’t yet tested every smart security system on the market. Other options, which we will be looking at soon, include smart, expandable and app-controlled systems from Nest, Blink, Abode, Somfy and Philips Hue, whose security devices integrate with its smart lighting products.

Nest is owned by Alphabet and therefore a sibling of Google and taps into the Google Home smart home ecosystem, with Google Assistant voice control.

Similarly, since Philips Hue is already such a big name in the smart lighting market, we’ll be reviewing its security products too. The Hue brand doesn’t offer a fully-fledged home alarm system, but its new security camera, door sensors and video doorbell, along with lighting that reacts to motion detection, could offer something unique among its rivals.

Professionally installed alarm brands to consider

All of the products highlighted in this article are intended for DIY installation. This makes them accessible and, while they come with instructions to help you install everything in the best location, their performance can vary depending on how and where each component is installed.

For a fully hands-off approach, where professionals take care of everything for you, there are other options to consider. These include Verisure, which works in a similar way to Simplisafe but requires professional installation. Verisure provides 24/7 UK-based monitoring, where trained staff respond to and verify alarm triggers, make contact with you, and call the emergency services and/or private security guard if required. There’s a smartphone app too, and even a deployable smoke screen to disorientate burglars.

Other options include companies you'll likely have heard of, since they’ve been in the security and home alarm business for years. These include ADT and Banham Security, and while they might lack the smart home gadgets of Ring and Eufy, they have masses of experience – case in point, Banham celebrates its centenary this year.

Professionally-installed systems tend to be more expensive than DIY alternatives. But with the extra cost comes reassurance that the various cameras, sensors and other components have been installed correctly, and in the best possible location. These systems also incur costs for their professional monitoring services – but this is where they really come into their own, offering a level of protection that Ring, Eufy, Tapo, Hue and others simply can’t match.

Why you can trust us

The Independent is committed to providing unbiased reviews and expert shopping advice across a range of home improvement products. Our team of experts has spent years testing and rating the latest smart home tech in our homes, gardens and under real-world conditions, so you can be sure our verdicts are authentic and based on personal experience with each product featured. When it comes to security systems, our expert testers consider everything from app features and ease of setup to ongoing subscription costs.
